lines.text: A coast that knew the slave ships, then a town founded for freedom. This is the story of Sierra Leone, through war and recovery.
From around 1670 a fort on Bunce Island in the river estuary held captives, and many thousands were shipped from there to America.
In 1792 freed black people from Nova Scotia landed nearby and founded Freetown, the Province of Freedom.
In 1827 Fourah Bay College opened there, the first university in West Africa.
Milton Margai, born in 1895, would become a doctor, and later the country's first prime minister.
As Britain pushed inland, it taxed every hut. In 1898 the people of the hinterland rose up against it.
Siaka Stevens, born in 1905, would later rule as president and turn the country into a one-party state.
In 1961 Sierra Leone became independent from Britain, with Margai as its first prime minister.
Julius Maada Bio, born in 1964, would serve in the army, and in 2018 be elected president.
In 1991 civil war broke out, fought over the country's diamonds. It raged for eleven brutal years.
When peace came in 2002, a special court was set up to try the leaders of the war.
Then Ebola came from neighbouring Guinea. In the largest outbreak ever seen, many of Sierra Leone's health workers lost their lives.
Founded as a home for the free, Sierra Leone has endured, and rebuilt.
